items.title: Twenty-Six Names for Affliction, Part One: Fetter, Flood, Yoke, Thorn-Stump, and More

items.zh: 煩惱差別者，多種差別應知。謂結、縛、隨眠、隨煩惱、纏、暴流、軛、取、繫、蓋、株杌、垢、常害、箭、所有、根、惡行、漏、匱、燒、惱、有諍、火、熾然、稠林、拘礙，如是等類煩惱差別。
items.en: As for the differences among afflictions: their many distinctions should be understood. They are called fetter, bond, latent tendency, secondary affliction, wrapping, flood, yoke, grasping, tie, hindrance, thorn-stump, stain, constant harm, and arrow — differences of this kind among the afflictions.

items.zh: 當知此中，能和合苦，故名為結。令於善行不隨所欲，故名為縛。一切世間增上種子之所隨逐，故名隨眠。倒染心故，名隨煩惱。數起現行，故名為纏。深難渡故，順流漂故故，名暴流。邪行方便，故名為軛。能取自身相續不絕，故名為取。難可解脫，故名為繫。覆真實義，故名為蓋。壞善稼田，故名株杌。自性染污，故名為垢。常能為害故，名為常害。不靜相故，遠所隨故，故名為箭。
items.en: It is called a fetter because it binds one together with suffering. It is called a bond because it prevents wholesome conduct from proceeding as one wishes. It is called a latent tendency because it is the dominant seed that trails after every being throughout the world. It is called a secondary affliction because it distorts and defiles the mind. It is called a wrapping because it manifests again and again. It is called a flood because it is deep, hard to cross, and carries one helplessly along with its current. It is called a yoke because it is the very mechanism of wrongdoing. It is called grasping because it seizes hold of one's own continuity without interruption. It is called a tie because it is so difficult to be freed from. It is called a hindrance because it conceals what is genuinely real. It is called a thorn-stump because it ruins a good field for planting. It is called a stain because its very nature is impure. It is called constant harm because it never ceases to injure. It is called an arrow because of its restless character and how relentlessly it trails after one.

items.title: Twenty-Six Names, Part Two: Root, Fire, Poverty, and Thicket — the List Closes

items.zh: 能攝依事，故名所有。不善所依，故名為根。邪行自性，故名惡行。流動其心，故名為漏。
items.en: Possession, root, misconduct, outflow, poverty, burning, distress, contention, fire, blazing, thicket, and obstruction — further differences of this kind among the afflictions. It is called possession because it lays hold of the very basis one depends on. It is called root because it is the source of every unwholesome deed. It is called misconduct because wrongful action is simply its own nature made visible. It is called outflow because it sets the mind adrift, flowing restlessly towards one object after another.

items.zh: 能令受用無有厭足，故名為匱。能令所欲常有匱乏，故名為燒。能引衰損，故名為惱。能為鬪訟諍競之因，故名有諍。燒所積集諸善根薪，故名為火。如大熱病，故名熾然。種種自身大樹聚集，故名稠林。能令眾生樂著種種妙欲塵故，能障證得出世法故，名為拘礙。
items.en: It is called poverty because it leaves one forever unsatisfied no matter how much is consumed. It is called burning because it makes what one desires seem perpetually lacking. It is called distress because it brings on sorrow and loss. It is called contention because it is the very cause of quarrels, lawsuits, and rivalry. It is called fire because it burns up the accumulated firewood of one's own wholesome roots. It is called blazing because it is like a raging fever consuming body and mind alike. It is called thicket because it produces one body after another, life after life, dense as a forest of trees. And it is called obstruction because it makes beings delight in exquisite sensory objects while blocking them from ever realising the transcendent path.

items.zh: 諸如是等煩惱差別，佛薄伽梵隨所增強，於彼種種煩惱門中建立差別。
items.en: All these differences among the afflictions were established by the Blessed Buddha according to whichever aspect happened to be most pronounced in each particular gateway through which affliction operates.

items.title: Each Name's Actual Headcount: Nine Fetters, Eight Wrappings, Five Hindrances, and More

items.zh: 結者，九結。謂愛結等，廣說如前。縛者，三縛。謂貪瞋癡。隨眠者，七種隨眠。謂欲貪隨眠等，廣說如前。隨煩惱者，三隨煩惱。謂貪瞋癡。纏者，八纏。謂無慚、無愧、惛沈、睡眠、掉舉、惡作、嫉妬、慳悋。暴流者，四暴流。謂欲暴流、有暴流、見暴流、無明暴流。如暴流，軛亦爾。
items.en: Fetter comprises nine fetters. Bond comprises three: craving, hatred, and delusion. Latent tendency comprises the seven latent tendencies. Secondary affliction comprises three: craving, hatred, and delusion. Wrapping comprises eight: lack of shame, lack of conscience, torpor, drowsiness, agitation, remorse, envy, and stinginess. Flood comprises four: the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of view, and the flood of ignorance. As with flood, so too with yoke.

items.zh: 取者，四取。謂欲取、見取、戒禁取、我語取。繫者，四繫。謂貪身繫、瞋身繫、戒禁取身繫，此實執取身繫。蓋者，五蓋，謂貪欲蓋、瞋恚蓋、惛沈睡眠蓋、掉舉惡作蓋、疑蓋。株杌者，三株杌，謂貪瞋癡。如株杌，如是垢、常害、箭、所有、惡行亦爾。根者，三不善根。謂貪不善根、瞋不善根、癡不善根。漏者，三漏。謂欲漏、有漏、無明漏。
items.en: Grasping comprises four: grasping desire, grasping view, grasping precept-and-vow, and grasping the doctrine of self. Hindrance comprises five: the hindrance of sensory desire, the hindrance of malice, the hindrance of torpor and sleep, the hindrance of agitation and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Thorn-stump comprises three: craving, hatred, and delusion — and as with thorn-stump, so too with stain, constant harm, arrow, possession, and misconduct. Root comprises the three unwholesome roots. Outflow comprises three: the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance.

items.zh: 匱者，三匱。謂貪瞋癡。如匱，如是燒、惱、有諍、火、熾然、稠林亦爾。拘礙者有，五拘礙。一、顧戀其身，二、顧戀諸欲，三、樂相雜住，四、闕隨順教，五、得微少善便生喜足。
items.en: Poverty comprises three: craving, hatred, and delusion — and as with poverty, so too with burning, distress, contention, fire, blazing, and thicket. Obstruction comprises five: attachment to one's own body; attachment to sensory desires; delighting in mixed company; lacking proper guidance; and feeling satisfied and ceasing effort after only a slight attainment.

items.title: Countless Faults, and Afflictive Defilement Is Fully Complete

items.zh: 煩惱過患者，當知諸煩惱有無量過患。謂煩惱起時，先惱亂其心，次於所緣發起顛倒，令諸隨眠皆得堅固，令等流行相續而轉。能引自害、能引他害、能引俱害；生現法罪、生後法罪、生俱法罪；令受彼生身心憂苦；能引生等種種大苦；能令相續遠涅槃樂；能令退失諸勝善法；能令資財衰損散失；
items.en: As for the faults of affliction: it should be understood that affliction carries countless faults. When affliction first arises, it disturbs the mind; next, it gives rise to a distorted grasp of its object; it makes the latent seeds ever more firmly entrenched; and it sets an ongoing current of similarly-flavoured activity in motion. It brings about harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both alike; it generates guilt in this present life, guilt in a future life, and guilt spanning both; it subjects one to bodily and mental suffering in the rebirth that follows; it brings about birth and every other kind of great suffering; it keeps one's continuum ever distant from nirvāṇa's own bliss; it causes the loss of superior wholesome states already attained; and it causes one's own wealth and resources to decline and be scattered.

items.zh: 能令入眾不得無畏，悚懼無威；能令鄙惡名稱流布十方，常為智者之所訶毀；令臨終時生大憂悔；令身壞已墮諸惡趣，生那落迦中；令不證得自勝義利。如是等過無量無邊。
items.en: It causes one to enter an assembly without confidence, timid and lacking any presence; it causes a base, disgraceful reputation to spread in every direction, drawing the constant censure of the wise; it brings on deep regret and sorrow at the moment of death; it causes one, once the body has perished, to fall into an unfortunate destiny, reborn in the hells; and it prevents one from ever realising one's own highest, ultimate good. Faults of this kind are without measure and without limit.

items.title: Karmic Defilement Opens: What Action Itself Actually Is

items.zh: 云何業雜染？嗢拕南曰：自性、若分別、因、位、及與門、增上品、顛倒、差別、諸過患。當知業雜染，由自性故，分別故，因故，位故，門故，上品故，顛倒故，差別故，過患故，解釋應知。
items.en: What is karmic defilement? A summary verse states: nature, and classification, cause and stage, and gateway, superior grade, distortion, differences, and faults. It should be understood that karmic defilement is to be explained through nature, through classification, through cause, through stage, through gateway, through superior grade, through distortion, through differences, and through faults.

items.zh: 業自性云何？謂若法生時，造作相起；及由彼生故，身行、語行於彼後時造作而轉；是名業自性。
items.en: What is karma's own nature? It is that, when this phenomenon arises, the mark of active volition arises; and, on the basis of that arising, bodily activity and verbal activity subsequently proceed to act it out. This is called karma's own nature.

blocks.text: Today finishes the account of affliction with its many names and its faults, and opens karmic defilement. The names come from the sūtras; each is a metaphor for one aspect of how affliction works. Read them slowly and notice which ones describe your own experience.
Affliction is called by many names in the sūtras, each with a reason:

items: a **fetter** (結), because "it binds one together with suffering";
a **thorn-stump**, "because it ruins a good field". Master Cháng Bǎi quotes a Chan verse: "The mind-field grows no weeds of ignorance; the nature-ground always blooms with wisdom";
a **fire**, "because it burns up the firewood of wholesome roots". Both teachers cite the saying: "One angry thought arises, and a million doors of obstruction open";

blocks.text: Venerable Miào Jìng's image for affliction as **obstruction**: a white ox and a black ox are tied together; neither ox binds the other; the rope between them binds both. So the eye does not bind form, nor form the eye; craving, the rope, binds.

The treatise gives the count for each name: nine fetters, three bonds, four floods, eight **wrappings** (纏), five **hindrances** (蓋), and so on. Master Cháng Bǎi explains the eight wrappings in pairs: lack of shame and lack of conscience block discipline; torpor and drowsiness block calm; agitation and remorse block insight; envy and stinginess block harmony with others.

"When affliction first arises, it disturbs the mind; next, it gives rise to a distorted grasp of its object; it makes the latent seeds ever more firmly entrenched; and it sets similar activity flowing." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Once affliction stirs, it never stirs for nothing. The first time it lasts five minutes; the next time, at least ten." Every affliction indulged makes the next one easier.

The faults continue: it brings the censure of the wise (Venerable Miào Jìng: being rebuked by fools may even show you are doing well; it is the wise whose censure matters), harms oneself and others, and leads to rebirth. Master Cháng Bǎi, relaying Venerable Miào Jìng: it usually harms both; conversely, someone who smiles like Maitreya cheers everyone who sees them.

Master Cháng Bǎi draws a structural point: "The root problem is affliction, not the deeds themselves; affliction is active, deeds are what it sets off." That is why the treatise treats affliction before karma.

Karmic defilement now begins. The nature of **karma** (業): "When this phenomenon arises, the mark of active **volition** arises; and on that basis, bodily activity and verbal activity proceed." Karma is volition (Day 4). Master Cháng Bǎi repeats the three steps: volition deliberates, decides, and impels.

Venerable Miào Jìng reads "bodily activity" and "verbal activity" (身行、語行) here in their technical sense: bodily formation is the breath; verbal formation is applied and sustained thought, which precede speech. Ru-Yi's translation reads them more plainly as bodily and verbal action. Either way, the definition is the same: karma begins as volition in the mind before it appears in body or speech.

Karma is classified in two ways: by the character of the person who acts, and by the nature of the deed. The second is the familiar **ten courses of action** (十業道), wholesome and unwholesome. Master Cháng Bǎi: they are called "courses" or "paths" because the ten unwholesome lead to the lower realms and the ten wholesome to humans and gods. Tomorrow the treatise portrays the person who kills.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why is affliction called a "fetter"?
options: it binds one together with suffering
quiz.why: "It is called a fetter because it binds one together with suffering." C is "bond," B is "tie" (hard to be freed from). Master Cháng Bǎi: a fetter involves five matters — what is bound, what binds, faults, outflow, and destination — joining one with suffering.

quiz.q: Affliction is "fire" because "it burns up the firewood of wholesome roots." What saying do the teachers cite?
options: "A single spark can start a prairie fire"
"One angry thought arises, and a million doors of obstruction open"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "'One angry thought arises, and a million doors of obstruction open.' Affliction saps the power of the good roots." Venerable Miào Jìng: "That burns your forest of merit." (The reading note renders it as one flash of anger burning down a forest of merit; the saying itself stresses the million doors.)

quiz.q: Affliction is called "obstruction." What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use?
options: a white ox and a black ox tied together — neither ox binds the other; the rope between, love of sense pleasure, binds you
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Two oxen, one white and one black, joined by a rope"; "it's your craving in between, love of the five pleasures, that binds you." The text: it makes beings delight in sense objects and blocks transcendent realisation. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Pixunji*: 拘 binds so one doesn't escape; 礙 blocks so one doesn't realise.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what does affliction do first when it arises?
options: first disturbs the mind, then distorts the grasp of its object, entrenches the latent seeds, and sets similar activity flowing
quiz.why: "When affliction first arises, it disturbs the mind; next, it gives rise to a distorted grasp of its object; it makes the latent seeds ever more firmly entrenched; and it sets an ongoing current of similarly-flavoured activity in motion." Then it harms self, others, and both; generates guilt now, later, and both; … up to preventing one's highest good.

quiz.q: The text says affliction "makes the latent seeds ever more entrenched." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain?
options: no affliction stirs in vain — the first time it lasts five minutes; next time at least ten
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Once affliction stirs, it never stirs for nothing"; "the first time it lasts five minutes and passes; now that won't do — now it takes at least ten." This echoes §14: each manifestation strengthens the seed.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, between affliction and karma, which is the root problem?
options: the root problem is affliction, not the deed itself — affliction drives, karma is driven
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The root problem is affliction, not the deeds themselves; affliction is active, deeds are what it sets off." Hence the treatise treats afflictive defilement before karmic. In fascicle 7 Venerable Miào Jìng likewise said: "What keeps you from liberation is affliction, not sin."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the nature of karma?
options: when it arises, the mark of active volition arises, and from it bodily and verbal activity proceed
quiz.why: "When this phenomenon arises, the mark of active volition arises; and, on the basis of that arising, bodily activity and verbal activity subsequently proceed to act it out." Master Cháng Bǎi: volition proceeds from deliberation to decision to impulsion; intention-karma is mental, post-intention karma is bodily and verbal.
